samples.text:
Today, many people prefer to buy almost everything online, such as clothes, electronic devices and even food, instead of going to the shops. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although it has some bad effects too.

The biggest advantage of online shopping is convenience. People can order things at any time of the day from their sofa, and the products are delivered to their door, sometimes on the next day. This is very useful for busy people, parents with small children and people who cannot walk easily. They do not need to drive to the city centre, look for a parking place and carry heavy bags.

Another advantage is that online shopping is often cheaper. Online stores do not need to pay rent for a big shop, so they can sell products for lower price. Customers can also compare the prices on different websites in a few minutes and choose the cheapest one. In addition, they can read reviews from other buyers, which help them to avoid buying bad products.

However, online shopping also causes some problems. Many small shops in town centres has closed because they cannot compete with big online companies, and some shop workers lost their jobs. Also, all the packaging and delivery vans create more rubbish and pollution. Sometimes the product looks different from the picture, and returning it take a lot of time.

In conclusion, I believe that buying things online is mainly a positive development, because it saves people time and money. However, people should also sometimes buy from local shops, so that town centres do not become empty.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas on convenience and price with some support · linking adequate but formulaic · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not reduce clarity.

samples.text:
Online shopping has grown so rapidly that many people now purchase the majority of their goods, from groceries to furniture, over the internet. Although this has made shopping more convenient, I believe that overall it is a negative development.

There is no doubt that buying online has clear advantages for consumers. It saves time, allows people to compare prices easily and gives access to a far wider range of products than any local shop could offer. For people with limited mobility or those living far from shopping centres, home delivery can be particularly valuable.

However, the decline of physical shops has serious consequences for local communities. As more spending moves online, independent retailers and even large chains are forced to close, leaving empty units in high streets and town centres. These places used to be not only somewhere to buy things but also social spaces where people met and interacted. When they decline, towns lose their character and jobs disappear, often in areas that already have limited employment opportunities.

In addition, the environmental cost of online shopping is often underestimated. Individual deliveries mean that large numbers of vans travel to people's homes every day, and each order usually comes with plastic and cardboard packaging. The ease of returning products also encourages people to order several items and send most of them back, which creates even more transport and waste. Furthermore, many warehouse and delivery workers face intense pressure and insecure contracts, which raise questions about the true cost of cheap and fast delivery.

In conclusion, while online shopping offers undeniable convenience for individuals, its effects on town centres, the environment and working conditions are harmful. For these reasons, I consider the shift towards buying most goods online to be a largely negative trend.
samples.why: Clear negative position after conceding benefits · ideas extended on community, environment and labour · logical progression · good vocabulary (high streets, insecure contracts) · mostly error-free with a minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
For a large proportion of consumers, the weekly trip to the shops has been replaced by a few minutes on a smartphone, with purchases arriving at the door within a day or two. This shift has undoubtedly come at a cost to traditional retail, but I believe that, on balance, it is a positive development.

The most obvious gains accrue to consumers. Online retail offers a range of choice that no single shop could match, together with the ability to compare prices and read other customers' experiences before buying. The resulting transparency places downward pressure on prices, which is of real value to households on tight budgets. Home delivery, moreover, has been transformative for people who find conventional shopping difficult, including elderly and disabled people and those in rural areas without nearby stores.

The internet has also lowered the barriers to starting a business. Whereas opening a shop requires premises, stock and a location with sufficient passing trade, a craftsperson or small producer can now reach customers across the country, or even the world, through a website or online marketplace. In this sense, online shopping has broadened, rather than merely concentrated, commercial opportunity.

The losses, however, are real. High streets in many towns have been hollowed out as shops close, taking with them jobs and a sense of place, and the proliferation of delivery vans and packaging has a considerable environmental impact. Yet town centres were already under pressure before online retail became dominant, and those that have reinvented themselves around leisure, services and community events show that decline is not inevitable. Environmental harm, likewise, can be reduced through consolidated deliveries and recyclable packaging.

In conclusion, although the move to online shopping has contributed to the decline of traditional high streets, it has given consumers greater choice, lower prices and easier access, and has opened markets to small producers. Overall, therefore, I regard it as a positive change.
samples.why: Clear positive judgement fully supported · original ideas (lower barriers to business) well extended · drawbacks weighed and qualified · skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (hollowed out, accrue) · error-free complex structures.
